subChunks.title: Statistics & Experimental Design for Scientists

storyBeats.txt: Theodora placed two stacks of papers on the table. "The first stack," she said, "contains published studies showing that a certain drug reduces cancer risk. The second stack contains studies showing it does not. Both are peer-reviewed. Both are statistically significant. And most of the first stack will turn out to be wrong."

"Statistics is not the language of certainty. It is the language of uncertainty — specifically, the language of how much confidence you should have in a result given the data you have, the noise in the world, and the number of times similar tests have been tried. A p-value of 0.05 is not a certificate of truth. It is a statement that, if the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would occur 5% of the time."

"Half of published findings in some scientific fields do not replicate. Not because scientists are dishonest, but because the incentive structures of academia reward positive findings, and the statistical tools are routinely misused or misunderstood. The most important scientific skill of the 21st century may be the ability to read a statistical result critically and ask: how many tests were run before this one, and is this finding real?"

subChunks.hookHtml: Statistics is the mathematical framework for making inferences from data under uncertainty. For scientists, statistical reasoning underpins every experiment: how to design studies that answer meaningful questions, how to analyse data without being misled by noise and bias, and how to communicate the strength of evidence honestly. Poor statistical practice — p-hacking, small samples, undisclosed multiple comparisons — is a major driver of the replication crisis. Understanding statistics is not optional for scientific literacy; it is foundational.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Descriptive Statistics

Measures of central tendency: Mean (arithmetic average) — sensitive to outliers. Median (middle value when sorted) — robust to outliers. Mode (most frequent value) — useful for categorical data. Which to use depends on data distribution: symmetrical → mean; skewed or outliers → median.

Measures of spread: Range (max − min) — simple, sensitive to outliers. Variance (σ²) — average squared deviation from mean. Standard deviation (σ or SD) — square root of variance, same units as data. Standard error of the mean (SEM = SD/√n) — estimates uncertainty in the sample mean; decreases with more data. Coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean × 100%) — relative variability, useful for comparing datasets with different means.

Normal distribution: Bell-shaped, symmetric about the mean. 68% of data within ±1 SD; 95% within ±2 SD; 99.7% within ±3 SD. Many natural measurements are approximately normal. Central Limit Theorem: sample means are approximately normally distributed regardless of the underlying population distribution, for large n. This justifies many parametric statistical tests.

Hypothesis Testing

Null hypothesis (H₀): The default assumption — no effect, no difference, no relationship. Alternative hypothesis (H₁): What you are testing for — an effect, difference, or relationship.

p-value: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed, assuming H₀ is true. p < 0.05 is the conventional threshold for "statistical significance" — arbitrary but widely used. Critically: a small p-value does NOT prove H₁ is true; it only says the data are unlikely under H₀.

Type I error (α): Rejecting H₀ when it is actually true (false positive). Rate = p-value threshold = 0.05 conventionally. Type II error (β): Failing to reject H₀ when H₁ is actually true (false negative). Statistical power = 1 − β — the probability of detecting a real effect if it exists.

Effect size: The magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size. A study can be statistically significant but clinically/practically trivial if the effect size is tiny (large n makes tiny effects significant). Report both: p-value (significance) AND effect size (importance).

Experimental Design

Independent variable: The variable manipulated by the experimenter. Dependent variable: The outcome measured. Control variables: Variables held constant to prevent confounding.

Control group: A group not receiving the experimental treatment — essential for comparison. Without a control, you cannot know whether changes would have occurred anyway.

Randomisation: Randomly assigning subjects to experimental groups prevents systematic bias (ensures groups are comparable at baseline). Blinding: Subjects don't know which group they're in (single-blind) or neither subjects nor experimenters know (double-blind) — prevents placebo effects and observer bias.

Replication: Repeating measurements within an experiment (n per group) and repeating the entire experiment independently. Within-experiment replication reduces random error; independent replication tests whether findings are real.

Sample size and power: Adequate sample size is needed to detect a real effect. Power analysis before the experiment estimates the n needed. Underpowered studies (too few subjects) miss real effects and produce unreliable estimates of effect sizes even when 'significant'.

Common Statistical Tests

t-test: Compares means of two groups. Paired t-test: same subjects in both conditions. Independent t-test: different subjects. Assumes approximately normal data or large n (CLT).

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Compares means across three or more groups simultaneously. Post-hoc tests (Tukey, Bonferroni) identify which pairs differ, correcting for multiple comparisons.

Chi-squared (χ²) test: Tests association between categorical variables (contingency tables) or goodness of fit to expected ratios. Non-parametric — does not assume normality.

Correlation (r): Measures strength and direction of linear association (−1 to +1). Pearson r: parametric, assumes normality. Spearman ρ: rank-based, non-parametric. Correlation does NOT imply causation.

Linear regression: Fits a line (y = mx + c) to quantify the relationship between predictor and outcome variables. R² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance explained. Allows prediction but assumes linear relationship and meets several assumptions (residuals normal, independent, homoscedastic).

Common Statistical Errors and Misuse

p-hacking: Running multiple analyses until p < 0.05 is found — inflates the false positive rate. Bonferroni correction: if k tests are run, use α/k as threshold per test to maintain overall α = 0.05.

HARKing (Hypothesising After Results Known): Presenting post-hoc hypotheses as if they were pre-specified. Legitimate only when clearly labelled as exploratory.

Survivorship bias: Only successful experiments are published; failed experiments disappear. Results may be systematically biased toward positive findings.

Confounding variables: A third variable associated with both the exposure and outcome, creating a spurious association. Example: shoe size predicts reading ability in children (both caused by age — a confounder).

Regression to the mean: Extreme values on one measurement tend to be less extreme on a second measurement, regardless of any treatment. Patients selected for being very sick often improve somewhat by the next measurement, even without effective treatment.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a p-value really means — not the definition people memorise, but what it actually tells you and what it definitely does NOT tell you.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A pharmaceutical company tests a new drug for reducing blood pressure. They randomly assign 60 patients to receive the drug and 60 to receive a placebo for 12 weeks. Mean blood pressure reduction: drug group = 8 mmHg (SD = 12), placebo group = 3 mmHg (SD = 11). The t-test gives p = 0.012. (1) State the null and alternative hypotheses for this test. (2) Interpret the p-value — what does p = 0.012 mean in this context? (3) Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the difference in means (use the approximation: 95% CI ≈ difference ± 2 × SEM_diff, where SEM_diff = √(SD₁²/n₁ + SD₂²/n₂)). (4) The company concludes the drug is 'highly effective'. Critique this conclusion — what additional information is needed to evaluate clinical importance? (5) If 40 different researchers each tested a different ineffective treatment at α = 0.05, how many would you expect to obtain 'statistically significant' results by chance?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) H₀: There is no difference in mean blood pressure reduction between the drug group and the placebo group (μ_drug = μ_placebo). H₁: There is a difference in mean blood pressure reduction (μ_drug ≠ μ_placebo) [two-tailed] — or directionally, μ_drug > μ_placebo [one-tailed].

(2) p = 0.012 means: if the null hypothesis were true (no true difference between drug and placebo), the probability of observing a difference at least as large as 5 mmHg (or larger) purely by chance would be 1.2%. This is less than the conventional threshold of 5%, so we reject H₀. It does NOT mean there is a 98.8% probability that the drug works, or that H₀ is false with 98.8% probability — p-values are not the probability that H₀ is true.

(3) Difference in means = 8 − 3 = 5 mmHg. SEM_diff = √(12²/60 + 11²/60) = √(144/60 + 121/60) = √(2.40 + 2.02) = √4.42 = 2.10 mmHg. 95% CI ≈ 5 ± 2 × 2.10 = 5 ± 4.2 = [0.8, 9.2] mmHg. The true mean difference is plausibly between 0.8 and 9.2 mmHg with 95% confidence.

(4) Critiques of 'highly effective': (a) Statistical significance ≠ clinical significance. A 5 mmHg reduction may be real (statistically), but clinical guidelines typically require ≥10 mmHg reduction for meaningful cardiovascular benefit — this effect may be too small to matter clinically. (b) The confidence interval (0.8–9.2 mmHg) is very wide — the true effect could be as small as 0.8 mmHg, which is clinically trivial. (c) Short-term (12-week) study — is the effect sustained? (d) Are there adverse effects that must be weighed against the modest blood pressure benefit? (e) Report effect size (Cohen's d ≈ 5/11.5 ≈ 0.43 — moderate) not just significance. The conclusion should state: 'statistically significant reduction of 5 mmHg (95% CI: 0.8–9.2 mmHg)' — not 'highly effective'.

(5) If 40 researchers each test an ineffective treatment at α = 0.05: each has a 5% chance of a false positive (Type I error). Expected false positives = 40 × 0.05 = 2 researchers. Two researchers would publish 'significant' results for ineffective treatments. If only positive results are published (publication bias), those 2 papers would be visible; the 38 negative results might not be. This is why meta-analyses and systematic reviews include all studies (published and unpublished) to avoid being misled by selective publication.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A researcher investigates whether a new teaching method improves science test scores. She assigns 30 students randomly to the new method and 30 to the traditional method. After 6 months: new method mean = 74 (SD = 10), traditional method mean = 70 (SD = 12). A t-test gives p = 0.09. (1) Should the researcher conclude the new method is ineffective? Explain what p = 0.09 means and why p > 0.05 does not prove the null hypothesis. (2) Conduct a power analysis critique: if the true effect size is about 4 points (Cohen's d ≈ 0.37), is n = 30 per group likely sufficient to detect this effect at 80% power? Qualitatively explain the relationship between sample size, effect size, and power. (3) The researcher decides to run 20 additional outcome measures (vocabulary, confidence, attendance, etc.) and reports that p < 0.05 for two of them. What statistical problem does this create, and how should it be corrected? (4) Design a stronger version of this experiment — describe at least four methodological improvements that would give more reliable results. (5) Explain why a randomised controlled trial (RCT) is considered stronger evidence than an observational study for establishing causal relationships, using this educational research as a context.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) p = 0.09 means: if the null hypothesis (no difference) were true, there is a 9% probability of observing a difference as large as 4 points by chance. This exceeds the conventional 0.05 threshold — we fail to reject H₀. HOWEVER: this does not prove the new method is ineffective. Failing to reject H₀ only means the evidence is insufficient to conclude there is a difference, not that there is no difference. There could be a real effect that the study lacked power to detect (Type II error). With only 30 students per group, the study may be underpowered for a modest effect size. The p = 0.09 result — close to but above 0.05 — is suggestive but inconclusive; reporting it as 'no effect found' is misleading. The appropriate conclusion: 'no statistically significant difference was found (p = 0.09); larger studies are needed.'

(2) For a true effect size d ≈ 0.37 (small-moderate) with n = 30 per group and α = 0.05 (two-tailed): power is typically ≈35–45% — far below the standard 80% threshold. This means a study this size would miss the real effect (if d = 0.37) about 55–65% of the time. Power analysis: power increases with (a) larger n — more data, smaller SEM, more ability to distinguish signal from noise; (b) larger effect size — bigger real differences are easier to detect; (c) smaller α — but lowering α reduces power. To achieve 80% power to detect d = 0.37 at α = 0.05, approximately n ≈ 120 per group would be needed. The sample was severely underpowered — the study should have been larger before being conducted.

(3) Multiple comparisons problem (Type I error inflation): with 20 additional tests each at α = 0.05, the probability of at least one false positive = 1 − (0.95)²⁰ ≈ 1 − 0.36 = 0.64 = 64%. Two significant results out of 20 tests is exactly what you would expect by chance (20 × 0.05 = 1 expected, and finding 2 is within random variation). Correction: Bonferroni correction — use threshold α/k = 0.05/21 = 0.0024 per test to maintain overall false-positive rate at 5%. Alternatively, use the False Discovery Rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) for less conservative correction. The reported 'significant' results for two outcomes should be presented as exploratory/hypothesis-generating, requiring confirmatory replication.

(4) Four methodological improvements: (a) Pre-registration: register the primary outcome (test score) and analysis plan before collecting data — prevents p-hacking and HARKing, and makes multiple comparisons explicit. (b) Larger sample size: conduct power analysis before starting; n ≈ 120 per group for 80% power at d = 0.37. (c) Blinding: blind outcome assessors (test markers) to group assignment to prevent unconscious bias in marking. Students cannot be blinded to teaching method, but assessors can be. (d) Longer follow-up: 6 months may not show durable learning benefits; 1–2 year follow-up would be more informative. (e) Active control (ideally): the traditional method group should receive the same amount of attention and teacher engagement as the new method group — to control for the Hawthorne effect (students performing better simply because they are being observed or receiving extra attention).

(5) RCT vs observational study: in an observational study of teaching methods, schools or teachers choose which method to use. This creates selection bias — schools that adopt new methods may differ systematically from those that don't (higher funding, better teachers, more motivated students). These confounders make it impossible to isolate the effect of the teaching method. In an RCT: random assignment to groups (new vs traditional method) ensures that, on average, students in each group are equivalent on all variables — observed and unobserved — at baseline. Any difference in outcomes can then be attributed to the teaching method itself, not to pre-existing group differences. Randomisation is the key mechanism for causal inference: it breaks the association between group membership and confounders. Observational studies can show correlation but cannot establish causation with the same confidence — even with sophisticated adjustment for known confounders, unknown confounders remain. The RCT is the gold standard for causal inference precisely because randomisation controls for all confounders simultaneously.
learningObjectives: Interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes correctly and explain what each does and does not tell us about a result.
Design a controlled experiment identifying independent, dependent, and control variables, and justify the use of randomisation and blinding.
Identify common statistical errors (p-hacking, multiple comparisons, HARKing, survivorship bias) and explain how they inflate false positive rates.
Explain why RCTs are stronger evidence for causation than observational studies and describe the role of confounding variables.
commonMistakes: Interpreting p < 0.05 as proving the hypothesis or meaning the result has a 95% chance of being true — p is the probability of the data given H₀ is true, not the probability that H₀ is false.

Confusing statistical significance with practical importance — large studies can detect statistically significant effects that are clinically or practically trivial; always report effect sizes alongside p-values.
Assuming p > 0.05 means 'no effect' — it means the evidence is insufficient to reject H₀; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, especially in underpowered studies.

Confusing standard deviation (SD) and standard error (SEM) — SD describes spread of individual data points; SEM describes uncertainty in the sample mean and decreases with more data; using SEM in bar charts makes effects look more precise than they are.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly interprets p-values and confidence intervals without the common misconceptions (p is not the probability H₁ is true; CI is not the range where 95% of data fall).
Designs a controlled experiment with appropriate controls, randomisation, blinding, and adequate sample size, with reasoning for each choice.
Identifies at least two sources of bias in a described study and proposes specific corrections.
Explains the multiple comparisons problem quantitatively (expected false positives) and applies Bonferroni correction.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: An alternative to frequentist hypothesis testing: instead of asking 'what is the probability of this data given H₀?' (frequentist), Bayesian statistics asks 'what is the probability of H₀ given the data?' — using Bayes' theorem to update prior beliefs with new evidence. Bayesian methods directly estimate the probability that a hypothesis is true and naturally handle multiple comparisons. Increasingly used in clinical trials, machine learning, and as an alternative to p-values in reporting research findings.

Pre-registration: researchers deposit their hypotheses, methods, and analysis plan in a public registry (OSF, ClinicalTrials.gov) before data collection. This prevents HARKing and p-hacking and distinguishes confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Open science practices (open data, open materials, pre-prints) increase transparency and replicability. The Centre for Open Science (COS) and various journals now require or reward pre-registration, representing a cultural shift in response to the replication crisis.

A quantitative synthesis of multiple studies addressing the same question — combining results to estimate an overall effect size with higher precision than any individual study. Uses statistical methods (random-effects models) to account for heterogeneity across studies. A well-conducted meta-analysis is the highest level of evidence in evidence-based medicine and science. Limitations: garbage in, garbage out — if individual studies are biased, meta-analyses of them will also be biased (publication bias, GIGO problem).

A crisis in multiple scientific fields (psychology, medicine, cancer biology, economics, nutrition science) in which many published findings fail to replicate when tested again by independent labs. Causes: p-hacking, HARKing, small samples, publication bias, undisclosed flexibility in analysis. The Open Science Collaboration (2015) replicated only 36–39% of 100 psychology studies. Responses include pre-registration, open data, registered reports, and larger collaborative replication projects. Understanding replication failure is essential for scientific literacy.

A confounder is a variable that is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, creating a spurious or distorted relationship. Classic example: ice cream sales and drowning deaths both peak in summer (confounded by hot weather). Controlling for confounders in observational studies: randomisation (RCT), matching, stratification, multivariable regression, propensity score methods, instrumental variables. Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) are a formal tool for identifying confounders, mediators, and colliders in causal reasoning.

questions.questionHtml: A study finds that children who eat breakfast have higher school test scores than those who skip breakfast (p = 0.001). Which conclusion is most justified from this finding alone?
options: Eating breakfast causes improved test scores — the p-value is very small, proving causation

There is a statistically significant association between eating breakfast and test scores, but the study does not establish causation — confounding variables (e.g. family income, parental education) may explain both habits
The result is definitely true and should immediately change school policy to require breakfast
Since p = 0.001, there is only a 0.1% chance the result is wrong
questions.correctAnswer: There is a statistically significant association between eating breakfast and test scores, but the study does not establish causation — confounding variables (e.g. family income, parental education) may explain both habits
questions.explanationHtml: A statistically significant association (p = 0.001) means the result is unlikely to be due to chance, but does NOT establish causation. This is an observational study — children chose whether to eat breakfast. Higher-income families are more likely to eat breakfast AND more likely to have educational resources, better schools, and parental engagement — all confounders. Statistical significance also does not mean the result is 'definitely true' (option C) — it means the association is unlikely to be due to sampling error; it could still be due to confounding. Option D is incorrect — p = 0.001 is the probability of observing this result if H₀ were true; it is NOT the probability that the result is wrong. To establish causation, a randomised controlled trial (providing breakfast vs not, randomising by family) would be needed.

questions.questionHtml: A clinical trial of a new drug tests 15 different outcomes (blood pressure, cholesterol, BMI, sleep quality, anxiety, depression, etc.). The drug shows p < 0.05 for 'sleep quality'. What is the probability of at least one false positive across all 15 tests, and what should the corrected significance threshold be?
options: P(at least one false positive) = 5%; corrected threshold = 0.05 as usual
P(at least one false positive) ≈ 54%; corrected Bonferroni threshold = 0.05/15 ≈ 0.0033
P(at least one false positive) = 15%; corrected threshold = 0.05/5 = 0.01
P(at least one false positive) = 1%; no correction is needed if all outcomes were pre-specified
questions.correctAnswer: P(at least one false positive) ≈ 54%; corrected Bonferroni threshold = 0.05/15 ≈ 0.0033
questions.explanationHtml: Multiple comparisons inflation: P(at least one false positive in k tests) = 1 − (1 − α)^k = 1 − (0.95)^15 ≈ 1 − 0.463 = 0.537 ≈ 54%. With 15 independent tests each at α = 0.05, there is a 54% chance that at least one 'significant' result is a false positive even when no drug has any real effect. Bonferroni correction: use α_corrected = 0.05/15 ≈ 0.0033 per test to maintain overall family-wise error rate at 5%. The 'sleep quality' p-value would need to be < 0.0033 (not just < 0.05) to be considered significant after correction. If the pre-specified primary outcome was not sleep quality, the finding should be labelled as exploratory and hypothesis-generating — requiring a dedicated confirmatory trial focused on sleep quality as the primary endpoint.

questions.questionHtml: A weight-loss supplement company cites a study showing their product produces average weight loss of 0.5 kg more than placebo over 12 weeks (p = 0.04, n = 800). They claim the product is 'proven to work.' A nutritionist argues this is misleading. Who is correct, and why?
options: The company is correct — p < 0.05 with n = 800 proves the supplement works; the large sample size confirms reliability

The nutritionist is correct — with n = 800, even a trivially small and clinically meaningless effect (0.5 kg over 12 weeks) becomes statistically significant; statistical significance does not imply meaningful weight loss or clinical benefit; effect size and practical significance must be assessed alongside p-values
The company is correct — any statistically significant result constitutes proof of effectiveness regardless of effect size
The nutritionist is correct — p = 0.04 is not sufficiently small to claim proven effectiveness; only p < 0.001 constitutes proof
questions.correctAnswer: The nutritionist is correct — with n = 800, even a trivially small and clinically meaningless effect (0.5 kg over 12 weeks) becomes statistically significant; statistical significance does not imply meaningful weight loss or clinical benefit; effect size and practical significance must be assessed alongside p-values
questions.explanationHtml: This illustrates the critical distinction between statistical significance and practical importance. With n = 800 (400 per group), the SEM of the difference is very small — even a tiny true effect (0.5 kg) can become statistically significant. But 0.5 kg over 12 weeks is clinically trivial: it is within normal daily weight fluctuation, below the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for obesity treatment (typically ≥5% body weight = 3–5 kg for most patients), and the confidence interval likely includes effects as small as a few hundred grams. A 'statistically significant' result only means the effect is unlikely to be zero — not that it is large enough to matter. Conversely, option D is wrong: p = 0.04 is a legitimate p-value; the threshold of 0.05 is conventional, and the problem is not the p-value level but the conflation of significance with effectiveness. The correct approach: report both p-value (0.04) and effect size (0.5 kg, 95% CI) and discuss clinical meaningfulness relative to the intervention costs, risks, and patient expectations.
